paragraphs.heading: What an aberration is
paragraphs.text: An aberration is a property of a lens, mirror or other optical system that keeps its image from being a true copy of the object. Depending on the type, the image may come out blurred, bent out of shape, or edged with colour fringes that the object does not have. Whatever the kind, a system with aberration gives an image that is not sharp.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: With an ideal lens, all the light leaving any one point on an object would meet again at one point in the image. Real lenses do not manage this, even when they are perfectly made. Aberration is that shortfall: light from one point of the object fails to gather at a single point after passing through. The cause is not faulty glass but the fact that paraxial optics, the simple theory used to predict how lenses behave, is not a fully accurate model of what they do to light.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds
paragraphs.text: Aberrations fall into two classes. Monochromatic aberrations come from the shape of the lens or mirror and happen with reflected and refracted light alike; they appear even with light of a single wavelength, which is where the name comes from. Chromatic aberrations come from dispersion, meaning that a lens's refractive index changes with wavelength. Because of this, different wavelengths focus at different points, so chromatic aberration disappears when only one wavelength is used.

paragraphs.heading: Effects left off the list
paragraphs.text: Defocus is technically the lowest-order aberration, but it is usually not counted, since moving the lens or the image plane to the focus fixes it. Piston and tilt shift where the focal point lands. They are not true aberrations either, because an otherwise perfect wavefront altered by them still forms a flawless image, only in a different place.

paragraphs.heading: Why perfection is out of reach
paragraphs.text: Classical optics pictures a perfect system in which rays from every object point unite again at an image point. Gauss's ideas of focal lengths and focal planes let you find the image for any system, but only if every ray makes an infinitely small angle with the optical axis. In practice that may not hold, so uncorrected systems give blurred images once the aperture or field of view passes certain limits. James Clerk Maxwell and Ernst Abbe showed that no optical system can meet the ideal, because it contradicts the basic laws of reflection and refraction. Gauss's theory is therefore a handy approximation, and aberrations always occur and may never be fully corrected.

paragraphs.heading: Taming it
paragraphs.text: Makers of optical instruments have to correct their designs to make up for aberration. A key part is the stop, or diaphragm: a hole, or the rim of a lens, that limits how wide a cone of light takes part in forming the image. The image of that stop formed by the parts in front of it is called the entrance pupil, and its position and diameter set how large the aberration is. Abbe also gave a rule called the sine condition; when it holds for all the rays forming a point, the aberrations that would otherwise spoil the points next to it are avoided.
